utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everyone. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-06-90-T, the Prosecutor versus Ante Gotovina, et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Could the witness be brought into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, while the witness is being brought, I just wish to inform Court I believe I miscalculated yesterday when I gave you my estimate. I should have said three to four sessions when I said two to three session. My apologies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we will see how matters developed and the time granted always depends on the efficiency with which the cross-examination is conducted. Still, there seems to be a chance, although less certain now, that we would conclude the testimony of this witness in two days. That might now -- we might need Friday as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Sacic. We will turn into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm very grateful to you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Ms. Mahindaratne, you may proceed. Mr. Sacic, will you now be cross-examined by Ms. Mahindaratne. Ms. Mahindaratne is counsel for the Prosecution. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Sacic. Now yesterday you discussed the advance of the special police forces during the period 4th August to 8th August. And it was your testimony that you were with the units that advanced towards Donji Lapac from Mazin through Gornji Lapac, and this is for the record, at transcript 27757. Isn't it correct that Mr. Markac, too, accompanied the force advancing towards Donji Lapac on 7th August?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Ms. Prosecutor, yes, he was there with me. But he was toward the middle or the rear of the column.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And is it correct that you and General Markac entered Donji Lapac about the same time, perhaps 15, or 10 to 20 minutes apart, but about the same time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, with a high degree of certainty I would say that what you have stated is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And this is on the 7th of August; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, as we said yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now the Trial Chamber has received evidence that once Donji Lapac was captured by the special police, a small logistics base was set up in Donji Lapac, and I refer to testimony of witness Janic P553, page 127, 139 to 140. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct, Ms. Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And the Trial Chamber also received evidence that a forward command post was set up in a house at the cross-roads between Gornji Lapac and Donji Lapac toward Kulen Vakuf; is that correct? For the record P553, page 166.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My apologies. I really apologise. Can you repeat your question. I didn't fully understand the first part of it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: The Trial Chamber has received evidence that a forward command post, a temporary forward command post was set up between Gornji Lapac and Donji Lapac on a cross-road.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I suppose you're discussing the 8th of August, after we entered Lapac. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: That's correct. After you entered Lapac, that's correct. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. At that point, I set up my forward command post precisely on -- at the location of Boricevac in the direction of Kulen Vakuf. But Mr. Markac was not there.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now do you recall after entering Donji Lapac on 7th August, on the 7th August itself, Mr. Markac had a meeting with member of the UNPROFOR in Donji Lapac? Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: About what time was that on the 7th? Approximately, roughly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I suppose it was around 14 -- or between 1430 and 1530. Perhaps even as late as 1600 hours. But I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now the Trial Chamber has also received evidence that on the 7th, after Donji Lapac was captured, there was a meeting conducted in Donji Lapac with the unit commanders, where you were present. Is that correct? Do you recall that meeting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I presumed this must have happened right after entering Donji Lapac, so it could have been 1430, 1500 hours. Certainly as a commander, as the Chief of Staff, the intention would to be immediately congratulate the subordinates on their great military success. That's for sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And was Mr. Markac present at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do suppose that he shared in the joy, just as I did, and that he was present.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now -- now, is it correct that the special police forces remained in that area, Donji Lapac, Gornji Lapac, Boricevac - pardon my pronunciation - till 9th August, until the area was handed over to the HV Home Guard units?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Esteemed Madam Prosecutor, from personal experience, I can tell that you very soon, some 30 or 40 minutes after our entry into Donji Lapac, I personally gathered all the available forces who were physically and mentally fit and upon receiving approval from General Markac, I set out for the state border with them. All the available forces, in other words, followed me, and the rest of the forces had to be deployed along strategic points along the length of the road, to ensure unhindered traffic and possibility for -- for our vehicles along Boricevac -- Donji Lapac, Boricevac, and Kulen Vakuf. And I'm convinced that in Donji Lapac, save for the logistics base which had several logistics officers and men in charge of maintaining the communications system and the security detail, there weren't more than 40 or 50 men there. But this is my approximation.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Sacic, I appreciate it's been some time since 1995, and perhaps your recollection isn't clear.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: If could I have a minute.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that part of the special police forces remained in Donji Lapac on the night of 7th August, not just a small handful of people but quite a significant number remained in Donji Lapac. On the night of 7th August.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Madam Prosecutor, from what I remember, all the important forces went along with me for that important mission of securing the state border. The men who remained behind were not that numerous, and they had to have been deployed around Donji Lapac. That's what I would say was the case since that would have been the logic employed by the commander, and this is confirmed by the facts.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Let me just remind you, Mr. Sacic, what you said in 2005, and that might refresh your memory.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And Madam Registrar, if could I have 65 ter, I believe, 7556, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: This is your 2005 video-recorded interview, Mr. Sacic. And if could you go to page 61. Page 61.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Very well. I can see it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Perhaps page 60, Madam Registrar. I'm sorry, we are on the correct -- correct page.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Do you note what have you said there. You are you asked the question, Did the special police of the MUP ever conduct any of -- I'm sorry. You go on to say: "No, we weren't in charge of that, and than night, we ... I left with the main part of the troops towards Boricevac, maybe some 100 to 200 people, no more than that stayed behind." And then you were asked: "And where were they? Where did you leave them? In Lapac or in the position where you had been?" And if could you move to the next page. Page 62. "No, they were around Lapac, in Lapac, around that. Around the house of the police station, there was the medical team ..." So, now do you recall about 100 to 200 members of the special police remained in Lapac the night of 7th August?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Fifty to a hundred, as is stated here. But today I would say even fewer. Well, in theory, complete with the medical teams, there could have been up to 100.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Okay. Is it correct that General Markac spent the night of 7th August in Donji Lapac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know about that. I'd -- I'm inclined to think that he did he not, that he had left, since he had other duties to attend to. I think -- no, I don't think. I'm sure that he went back to the Gracac staff, since there were major activities taking place on that day. But these are only my assumptions. I didn't see him. I certainly did not see him spend the night -- stay behind and spend the night in Lapac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne, what we see on our screen now, on the 27th, the interview on the 27th, that is, the first day of the two days of interviews. I see on line 12 that Mr. Sacic answered the question in which the name of Mr. Markac appears, although the interpretation was, to some extent, inaudible, and in order to better understand this portion of the statement, where, apparently, those who were transcribing could understand, could hear the answer in the original language, I'd like to seek whether we could have access to the content of that. And I would invite a native speaker just to read slowly the first part of the answer so that we know at least what we're talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, might I just suggest that the witness just read lines 12 through 15 himself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Can you see on your screen, Mr. Sacic --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can see it, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Can you please slowly read what was recorded at the time as your answer, starting on line 12, continuing to line 15. Could you slowly read that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "And I don't know anything else because I really left quite soon. You should further discuss it with General Markac, with the police, when the ordinary police arrived, whether it was that same evening, when the Croatian Army arrived in Lapac, that's another matter that needs to be looked into. I don't know that."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, when I questioned you about if Mr. Markac spent the night of 7th August in Donji Lapac, you said that he probably did not. Let me remind you, Mr. Sacic, what you have said in 2005 when you were interviewed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, if I could have 65 ter 7576, please. And if you could take me to page 121. 121.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: You can you follow, Mr. Sacic, this is what you say: "And I was with the troops all the time, and even General Markac was with me later on. In the afternoon, when we arrived Gornji and Donji Lapac and I spent the night in a village there, Boricevac, there, towards border with Bosnia and Herzegovina, towards Kulen Vakuf ..." And if you could take the page down: "And General Markac stayed in Donji Lapac." And you further go on to speak about this.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: If we could go to 65 ter 7556, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Let me show you other parts of your statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: This is the same interview, Mr. Sacic, but different tapes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, yes. Fine, what is it that I have to confirm?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... let me also show you. And then if you could move to page 33 of this section: "And when you arrived in Donji Lapac, do you recall what time of the day it was? "Yes, of course. It was afternoon. It was 4, 4.30, sometime between 4.00 and 4.30." And Madam Registrar, if you could go down. "Okay, and would it be fair to say based on what you previously said that General Markac wouldn't have gone into Donji Lapac until it was considered secure, safe?" "That's not the rule." And if could you move on to the next page: "He didn't really have a choice. He couldn't go back anymore. He had to go where the majority of forces were. He couldn't stay in Gornji Lapac, so he came to Donji Lapac. They were bombing there, and he couldn't go to Gornji Lapac. He wanted to come to Donji Lapac."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: So in 2005, what you said is that Mr. Markac stayed back in Donji Lapac. But today you're saying that that wasn't the case. So do you want to reconcile your testimony with what you said back in 2005?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I will, yes, Madam Prosecutor. When I was giving my statement at the time, what's not certain is whether I was really put specific questions. But I can tell you that what I've stated today is something that I'm deeply convinced of. General Markac had no reason whatsoever to stay in Donji Lapac throughout that time, and he definitely -- I'm sure he did not say there, and I'm sure that he went back the same evening as I was advancing toward Kulen Vakuf. He, for a number of other reasons related to the Main Staff, had to leave Donji Lapac because there was no reason for the Commander-in-Chief to stay there. I was speaking about all -- the overall forces in general who remained under my command until the 9th of August in that area.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Very well. Now, did you learn that, at some stage, after special police entered Donji Lapac that it was destroyed? That houses and property were set on fire.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When -- while I was there, up until the 9th of August, and I say this with great certainty. And I mentioned this yesterday, there was no need for me at all to enter Donji Lapac, so I didn't observe that because I had to be in my staff, the forward command post, I had to be there physically because we were under attack, and I had there everything that I needed, logistics support and so on, because all of that was -- all those requests would come to me, so that I really did not know anything about the destruction. That was something that was not the focus of my interest. My task there was crucial to repeal the attack and to prevent the advance of -- of some troops of the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, can we move on this same document to page number 57, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Sacic, and you were questioned about this issue in 2005. And let me read back what you said then. Page 57. This is what you said: "Later, several days later, on 9th, I heard it was burned, that something was burning there." "On the 9th, yes." "But the special police most certainly did not take part in that, but I believe that whilst the special police were on the outskirts of the town and certainly some of them were going into the town, when the town was damaged."

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And then if could you move to page 59.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, sorry to interrupt. For the sake of completeness, I think we should read line 30, or the English translation of line 30 of that previous page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you please follow that suggestion.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. At page 30 it says: "Probably you, because of that exchange of fire, that artillery exchange of fire." That was at line 30. And if could you move to page -- not 60, page 59. 59. You say Donji Lapac was -- you were asked the question: "Donji Lapac was destroyed, though?" And your answer is, next page, please: "That's fact now. And now it is well known." "I heard that, I heard that now, later." So, Mr. Sacic, this is on video record of what you said in 2005, and your testimony is that on the 9th, you heard that Donji Lapac was burning, and then you went on to say that it's a fact that it is destroyed. So can you explain to the Trial Chamber as to why you have since then changed your mind about what you knew then.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I haven't changed my mind. I personally saw the burning, and I said that yesterday before this Chamber. I saw a building that was on fire. It was the police station building. I also saw that there were some vehicles on the side of the road because of the artillery attacks. And also that there were -- there was glass, broken glass. But it wasn't destroyed, and it was -- the road was passable. However, I said there that that was the fact then, which is what I learned much later from newspaper articles and so on. So that's what I meant when I said "it's a fact that it was destroyed." But, on the 9th, the 8th or, rather, the 9th, as you say, I say that I probably didn't have any direct knowledge, any personal knowledge, because I don't even remember going to Donji Lapac then. Simply, there was no need for me to go there. But after some time, whether this was already in Gracac when I was at the headquarters or maybe a month, two, or three later, I learned from reports probably that it had been thoroughly destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Sacic, I didn't suggest that on the 9th you saw Donji Lapac burning, but what you had said in 2004 -- five was that you heard -- on the 9th, you heard that Donji Lapac was burning. That -- that's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That could be correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I take it that when you say "that could be correct," that is correct. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. That someone could have said that to me, that is probably correct. That someone came up to me and said, Listen, there is something burning in Gracac, that this happened on the 8th or 9th, yes, that could be so. That -- it's probably how it was.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Sacic, I think you said in your answer that there is something burning in Gracac. I believe you meant to say Donji Lapac.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Donji Lapac. I apologise. Donji Lapac.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, having heard this, and you said later on you learnt that Donji Lapac was thoroughly destroyed, did you or did General Markac conduct any inquiries as to who burnt or destroyed Donji Lapac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I certainly was not the one. Whether the General did, you have to ask him. But I know for a fact that I did not take any action in that respect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Sacic, if you have any knowledge, even if it would be hearsay, we'd like to hear your answer. You don't have to tell Ms. Mahindaratne who she -- she should ask this question. She asked the question from you. You didn't investigate, from what I understand.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But have you any knowledge, either direct or indirect, in relation to any inquiries conducted by others than yourself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then please tell us what you know about it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I know, because I think I heard this information in -- at the headquarters in Gracac or in Zagreb, after a while, perhaps three or four weeks later, I learned from the chief of logistics, Mr. Branislav Bole, who was, undoubtedly, in Donji Lapac on that day, who said that, on that day, sometime in the evening, this was late, which means that I wasn't there, but this is all second-hand information, hearsay. This is according to how Bole remembered that. So members of the Croatian Army came from somewhere, and they were very noisy. Allegedly, they were even surprised, these Croatian Army members, that our logistics unit was there. So that would be all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Sacic, the question was about whether you are you aware of any inquiries or any -- I understood - Ms. Mahindaratne, please correct me when I'm wrong - whether in any way this was investigated, whether any inquiries were made as to who did this. Now your answer was what you heard a couple of weeks after that --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I don't know. That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Sacic, you said three or four weeks later Mr. Bole was talking about what happened in Donji Lapac that night. So is it correct that there was a discussion at the Gracac lawyers about the burning in Donji Lapac? Is that the result of Mr. Bole talking about as to how this came about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's possible. And I say this was just a possibility, that this was either in Gracac or in Zagreb. But where exactly, I can't tell you, and I can't even tell you when exactly this happened, whether, as I said a few moments ago, whether this was immediately following the events or a couple of weeks later, I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Sacic, my question is, what led to Mr. Bole giving that explanation? Was there some query made or a discussion about Donji Lapac burning on 7th night either by you or someone else, General Markac, the inner control branch? Was there some discussion? That's what I'm asking you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Now I understand what you mean. Well, I assume that I must have asked Bole something about it, so I would have had some information about Gracac being in this condition. In other words, that it was burning, and I assume that it was a logical question, that it sounded logical -- that it was a logical question for chief, Bole, because he was the only one who was there, as far as I know. He did not speak of this on his own initiative, spontaneously.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Again, Mr. Sacic, you mentioned the word "Gracac" there. Information about Gracac. I presume you meant to say Donji Lapac.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, of course, Donji Lapac was on fire. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: So --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I will do my best to be as focussed as I can, but I can't promise that I won't misspeak again. But please correct me.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now you just said that, chief Bole was the only one who was there, as far as I know. Are you not aware that Mr. Janic, the chief of the anti-terrorist department, was present in Donji Lapac the night of 7th August?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, he wasn't with me at the time. However, as the other forces, as I mentioned today, were deployed along the road, it is quite possible that he, as my deputy, actually commanded those forces on the road between Gornji and Donji Lapac, although, frankly speaking, I can't really remember that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, you said, Mr. Sacic, that to your knowledge there was no investigation into the burning in Donji Lapac. Do you know if, in fact, at least a report was called from either Mr. Bole or Mr. Janic or any other person who was in Donji Lapac regarding the burning?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that during my preparations for this evidence, I ran into -- I found the report by Branislav Bole while reviewing the documents and archives where he said -- where he described the arrival of the Croatian Army forces in Lapac. However, I certainly do not remember such a report from 1995 or 1996. I did not notice it then. Such a report does exist, and it is in the special police archives. It would have had to be there.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: So, to your knowledge in 1995, you didn't see this report, Mr. Bole's report? You saw it only in preparation for this evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I'm almost absolutely sure that that's how it was. I'm almost sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, may I have P586, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Sacic, is this the report you saw in the archives when you were preparing for this examination, where you said this was -- you haven't seen this in 1995?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, this is it, certainly. No doubt about it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, this report is addressed to you. And it is your testimony that this report was not submitted to you in 1995?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And that's quite understandable. Some time had elapsed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Sacic --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And I'm glad that you have it here --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Sacic, my question is, it was not submitted to you. I mean you don't have to give me explanations as to why that could be. Just, yes or no.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If it says that it was filed in Zagreb on the 2nd of November [as interpreted], 1995, to the chief Zeljko Sacic, that must have been shown to me, it must have been on my desk.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: On the 2nd of October.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And I thank you for refreshing my memory.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr Sacic, my question is today, don't speculate whether it was on your table or what the document says. Your -- you do not have a recollection of receiving this document in 1995. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, that's not correct. Now you've just refreshed my memory, and now I believe that I did receive it. In fact, I'm quite certain because Bole would not have written it subsequently.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Sacic, I asked you several times about whether you had received a report from Mr. Bole. You vehemently denied and you, in fact, testified here just now that you saw this document in the archives when you were preparing for this examination which you said that did you not see in 1995. Now suddenly your memory seems to have --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: -- been jogged to the point you suddenly remember this.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's right, and that is very logical. You recall that I said that she had reported this to me orally, so I did have some recollection, and I even cited from the contents. But it's illogical. And there is really nothing at issue here. There is no reason why I would try to conceal anything, and I appreciate your jogging my memory, because, had I wanted to actually conceal this, then in I wouldn't even have mentioned that Bole told me something about it orally.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, do you recall receiving a report from Mr. Janic about what happened in --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't remember. I don't remember. Certainly not.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, may I have D556, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: When you said "certainly not," did you intend to say that you certainly did not see it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That I don't remember, that I can't recall. Certainly can't recall, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Sacic, this report you can see, by Mr. Janic is addressed to you, but you have -- you said you haven't received it. And you didn't know about --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no, I have to intervene here. I said that I could not remember it, and that's a major distinction. As I can see, I did receive it, but I could not actually remember it today.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Sacic, there you can see on the top right-hand corner of that document there is an handwritten -- there's handwritten text. And it says: "Call General Markac and informed him of ..." And perhaps it is more legible in the Croatian, the original document. Do you know whose handwriting is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Certainly. That is unfortunately my handwriting, and I really have a bad handwriting.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: So -- now, I asked you about discussions about what happened in Donji Lapac on 7th, whether Mr. Markac and -- whether you discussed, Mr. Markac discussed, whether someone else discussed, and you could not recall. Now can you explain to the Trial Chamber why that entry means.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: What exactly did you inform Mr. Markac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, on what is in this document, obviously, that's what I informed him because it says there, "Call General Markac and inform him on the incident, the burning." And certainly it is quite certain that I did not keep this in my desk drawer. Although I don't recall exactly the very act and how I informed him, how I did that. But it says here, in my handwriting, that I did do it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: So the reason for you to inform Mr. Markac about the content of this report is obviously because Mr. Markac and you must have had a discussion about the burnings in Donji Lapac on 7th August night; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the 7th of August, on the 7th of August, you mean?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Sacic, my question is: the reason you informed Mr. Markac the contents of this document is because there must have been a discussion between you and Mr. Markac about what happened in Donji Lapac on the 7th night, not that your discussion took place on the 7th August, but what happened, the incident of burning that took place on 7th August.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Well, I suppose that that's exactly the reason, because obviously this concerned me. Someone had advised me of this. Someone had obviously told me to seek reports on why and how it was captured, and how the Croatian Army joined up the special -- with the joint -- special police, and whether, on that occasion, there were -- there was some torching or some problems, and obviously that was the reason why such -- these reports were submitted to me. And it is certain that that triggered my, as it says there, "call General Markac," calling him to inform him of it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Okay. Now, to your knowledge, was there ever an investigation by any element of the Ministry of Interior into -- as to -- to -- establish as to who burnt the property in Donji Lapac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If we could call this report from Bole and from Janic, those would be arguments confirming that there was an on-site investigation initiated, but whether --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Sacic, please, I'm not asking you to analyse these documents. My question is: to your knowledge, was there an investigation conducted by any element of the Ministry of Interior, either fundamental police, crime police, or the special police as to what happened in Donji Lapac? That's my question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Prosecutor. As far as I know, it wasn't, but my knowledge has to do with what I can recall.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Sacic, I am working against the clock, so I would be grateful if you confine your responses to my question. Now --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I will do my best.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, the Trial Chamber has received evidence, Mr. Sacic, that 90 per cent of the houses along the road between Gracac and Donji Lapac had been burnt down and destroyed, and, in fact, members of the special police were present in the area while dwellings were still ablaze. I'm referring to evidence at -- at P2359, paragraph 42, transcript page number 16761, 764, 765, and 770.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kuzmanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Is that between Gracac and Donji Lapac? Is that the question?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: That's correct. If Mr. Kuzmanovic is going to say anything, I -- maybe it might be proper for the witness not to be present.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second. I think that Mr. Kuzmanovic was verifying whether he well understood your question. Is that ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Whether there's any possible confusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And the question has been answered. Could you please repeat the question so that the witness can answer the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Sacic, did you hear my question? Shall I ask again? The Trial Chamber has received evidence that 90 per cent of the houses along the road between Gracac and Donji Lapac had been burnt down or destroyed and members of the special police were seen present in the area, while the -- the houses, the property, were still ablaze. Now, your testimony is that you, in fact, advanced with the units. And my question is: did you -- what did you do about this? Did you see special police members standing in front of burning houses?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, absolutely not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kuzmanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I think the methodology is that the witness should not put someone else's testimony before him without asking him those questions first. I think that is what we have been doing in the past, and I know there have been citations to the record that counsel has made. I don't necessarily disagree with providing citations to the record, but I think the procedure is to ask the witness first what his recollection was and then put the information that the counsel wants to put to the witness on what other people said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, it could be debatable whether the earlier testimony of the witness about damage, whether that would already cover this. That is not entirely clear. But, Ms. Mahindaratne, you're encouraged as is the practice before this Chamber to first ask the witness without referring to evidence the Chamber has received. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Before the break I just have one more question.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Sacic, 90 per cent is a significant amount of property that one would not miss out if it is destroyed. Can you explain to the Trial Chamber as how you, you know, having advanced with your units, could miss out such a large amount of destruction?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Very simply, it means that they did not happen at the time I was there or when I was going back. That could be the only reason, otherwise I would have observed them.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Did you see or did hear about such a destruction later on, having gone back to Gracac after your work in the area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did, but not in Gracac. In 1996, 1997, and 1998, this was widely written about in Croatia. But at the time I was there, thank God, this was not to be seen where I was moving about. But if 90 per cent of the houses were aflame whilst I was present there, well, I would have gone up in flames together with them, I suppose.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I believe that is a suitable time for the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll have a break, and we will resume at quarter past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, excuse me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Before we continue, I need to make -- put something on the record with regard to the citations provided by counsel in one of the previous questions. If that's okay with you, Your Honour. I have an objection about the methodology under which this questioning began, and I have the relevant examples to show why this questioning is misleading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Kuzmanovic, if it is about summarising what the Chamber received as evidence, where Ms. Mahindaratne made reference to transcript pages and to certain documents, documentary evidence, then we'd like to hear from you at a later stage, not necessarily now where she went wrong. I hope that you first did inform her that you were dissatisfied with the examples you want to give to the Chamber. Now if there is any issue about that, you know that we usually take the following, a party who puts to a witness what was received as evidence by this Chamber, if there is any doubt as to the accuracy of the representation, then, immediately intervene and ask the party to put to the witness exactly what the evidence was. If it is -- I did understand that at least at one of the occasions where Ms. Mahindaratne gave rather detailed sources, it was a P exhibit number, it was a witness statement, she referred to the paragraph, she further referred to certain transcript pages. Then if there is any reason not to accept that as a sufficient -- sufficiently accurate reference, then we go to the source, and then we look at that. If that is the issue --

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: This is the issue, Your Honour, and it took me a while, obviously, to look, and what's I was doing over the break, looking at the transcript references and at the P exhibit reference, referring to the testimony of Witness 82. And it's not that -- the question which is the Trial Chamber has received that 90 per cent of the houses --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I thought that you would -- I also tried to immediately find the sources, and my problem is that I have to do other things at the same time apart from doing my background research. Ms. Mahindaratne could, we -- Mr. Kuzmanovic, as matters stand now, I take it that we'll have a look that those sources. Ms. Mahindaratne is now put on notice that there was a problem. We will resolve that in the course of the further examination of the witness. And, Ms. Mahindaratne, please carefully consider whether the way in which you presented that evidence, and it was P25 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 2359 -- oh, now our transcriber has simultaneously three numbers, and she wonders whether we were all -- it was 23.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'll check that. And Ms. Mahindaratne, you are put on notice that whenever you summarise in a question the evidence, that you should do it with 100 percent accuracy. If not, first of all, there will be objections, and, of course, what the Chamber expects the parties to do is, on the one hand, that are you really accurate, and, on the other hand, that if it is a fair summary that there will be no objections, so not unnecessarily go back to the source. But it is up to you. You'll find the objections which you have asked for. You are advised not to ask for any objections.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Advice taken, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kuzmanovic, if could you also -- because then I would find time. The paragraph was 40 ...

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: 42, Mr. President. And can I repeat the PD [sic] transcript reference numbers if Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, I can look them up, and -- in e-court. So perhaps we first proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Sacic, one -- just one question on that previous subject we were on. Now we saw from Mr. Bole's and Mr. Janic's report that there was a suggestion that the destruction in Donji Lapac -- the persons responsible for the destruction there Donji Lapac could be members of the HV. Now, did you or Mr. Markac report that to the military police or any military authority?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not, most certainly. That's the short answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Mr. Sacic, is it correct that members of the special police are not authorised to take or drive civilian vehicles? In their official capacity, in the course of -- you know, after Operation Storm, in the liberated territory, the abandoned civilian vehicles, were they authorised to take them or drive them, use for their purposes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They would have to provide substantial reasons for it. For instance, that it was for the purposes of the service, that they had to reach a location urgently and didn't have their own means of transportation, and they could use the vehicle only for as long as it was urgently needed. And this is provided for in the Law on Internal Affairs which relates to the use of citizens's vehicles, but these are exceptions.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Was there any -- any situation or any arrangement within the special police where members of the special police were asked to drive abandoned vehicles from one location to the other? Not for urgent purposes but just drive them to designated locations.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This was possible. However, this went through our logistics department, Mr. Branislav Bole, or, if some other special police unit was involved of a certain police administration, then, notification had to be made immediately of a vehicle which was in disrepair or left abandoned by the roadside, the individuals involved could make the vehicle operational, make sure that it is up and running, but the relevant police administration had to be informed of it forthwith.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now you were shown yesterday some photographs by the Chambers one picture was of a person hot-wiring a car.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And, Madam Registrar, if I could have P234, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And, in fact, you were shown -- do you recall that you were shown those photographs even in 2005 by the investigators of the Office of the Prosecutor. Do you recall seeing this -- one picture is on the screen now. And if we could --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And, Madam Registrar, if we could move to the next page.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Do you recall you were shown this picture? And if you could also --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, of course, I do remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And if you could move to the next picture also, please. Do you recall when you were shown these pictures that you informed the -- the investigator of the Office of the Prosecutor that members of the special police were not authorised to use civilian vehicles, unless in an emergency to transport wounded civilians?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, you can see that what I've been saying today is along those lines. In other words, yes, I do remember that. But if I may add the following. The lawyer who was with me at the time reacted to this - I remember this well - and asked the investigators when these photographs were made. The investigator told us that it was either on the 7th or the 8th of August, I'm not sure. In any event, the upshot is that I was not physically in Gracac at the time. I can -- I'm telling you this just as an aside, to let you know what happened during the interview.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Sacic, this Trial Chamber has received evidence that members of the special police were seen looting in the centre of Gracac on 8th August, and I'm referring to P321, paragraph 29, paragraph 30, and 31 -- I'm sorry, paragraph 30 and 31.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kuzmanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm not asking the questions here, but the question should be, Did you see anyone living in Gracac? And depending on what the answer is, then confront him with the evidence, supposedly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne, isn't it true that I referred to the practice in this courtroom -- [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I apologise, Mr. President, that was -- I will rephrase, and I'll get back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so. And as I said before, objections are best avoided by not asking for them.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: My fault. My apologies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Sacic, are aware of members of the special police looting in Gracac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Never. Never.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: This Trial Chamber has heard evidence that, on the 8th of August, members of the special police were seen looting in the centre of Gracac where, in fact, the special police headquarters is located. So what do you have to say about that? How is that that type of conduct could occur in the very location where your headquarters are located?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I simply I can't believe that this would be true. That's my response. They had a very clear instruction that they should not engage there looting and that they should conduct themselves in accordance with the rules of engagement and with laws of war and laws applicable in peacetime. If anybody did do this, then he did it without any approval. These were looters who should have been sanctioned.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And to your knowledge was any member of the special police sanctioned, punished for looting in Gracac or anywhere else during Operation Storm -- or, actually, after Operation Storm was completed, after the territory was liberated?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't remember. Truly, I can't recall there having been proceedings against a member of the special police and who had been found to have looted through a disciplinary proceedings. Perhaps the Zadar police station may have had such proceedings, but I don't remember anything else. It could have been something connected with the Zadar special police unit, but I can't really be sure whether this happened at that time and at that place, that a commander punished his member of the special police unit for having done something, this is not something that I can remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Sacic, do you recall seeing property in Gracac, in Gracac or outside Gracac, burning after the special police headquarters was set up on the 5th?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the outskirts, well, when I arrived there on the night of the 5th, a house could be seen on fire at night-fall somewhere out in the outskirts. You couldn't see the house. You could see the fire. Our commanders received clear instructions. General Markac told me expressly, and I told all the commanders expressly in Gracac when -- as soon as we gathered there, that no cases of looting, torching, or anything else irregular would be tolerated, that regular security needs to be enforced as soon as possible. So now the special units arrived on either the 5th late during the day or early on the 6th. I know that the military police arrived on the 6th, and the commander of the military police came to report to me as a chief of the sector. I told him the same, that the military police should make sure that no sort of arson or anything like that occur.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Sacic, the Trial Chamber has received evidence, in fact, that on the 8th of August, there were -- there was property burning in Gracac as well as on the outskirts of Gracac. Now what do you have to say about that. Because not withstanding you are saying, it seemed to have continued even on the 8th of August?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kuzmanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry to intervene, Your Honour, we now have now -- the Trial Chamber has received evidence and would like to know specifically -- [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne, could --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: P321, paragraph 29.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you put that to the witness. You will understand that I have no clear recollection what P231 [sic], paragraph 29 says.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: P321, Mr. President, that is Mr. Vanderostyne's statement. I will be very precise.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. If you put to him what he says in paragraph 29, if you put that to the witness, then ...

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. President. P321. It's should be P321.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then it is ... yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Your Honour wishes me to read exactly that, or can I make just make the suggestion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, there are two ways of doing it: either to read the relevant passage to the witness, or to read it for yourself and make sure there is no inaccuracy in the summary of that evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Sacic, a witness has testified to this effect before the Trial Chamber: "Upon entering Gracac I saw several houses that were just set on fire. There was smoke all over the outskirts." Now, this is on 8th August. Can you please explain to the Trial Chamber as to how three days after the completion of the offence property could be burning in Gracac and on the outskirts of Gracac notwithstanding that the special police headquarters was located in Gracac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Prosecutor. This is surprising, indeed, that houses were on fire. But I cannot answer your question why this happened because I wasn't there. And nobody informed me at a later stage that these houses had been on fire there. If there was no military activity where houses were used as shelter which would lead to them being on fire, then they should not have been aflame. Or unless there had been artillery fire or unless an installation was there. But what -- all these stories are perhaps superfluous now.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: To your knowledge, were any investigations conducted by the fundamental police, or the crime police, or the special police about destruction and burning of property in Gracac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I am aware of it but not from personal experience. I wasn't present, but I heard most definitely that some investigating bodies, either the ordinary uniformed police or the military police, arrested an arsonist in Gracac who had been driving in a vehicle and caused a house to be on fire. When did this happen? On the 8th, I'm not sure. Maybe it did; maybe not. When he was arrested, I don't know. But this is a story that stayed with me, and it should be recorded somewhere. There should be a record of it somewhere of this individual on a motorbike, in fact, so --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And from what you heard was that individual member of the special police or civilian police or the military or a civilian?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I couldn't really tell with certainty whether he was a special police, a soldier, or a civilian. But I know for certain that he was on a motorbike because that was as much a bizarre detail, so it stayed with me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kuzmanovic -- yes, Mr. Mikulicic. I'm still thinking in -- in what I heard from the Markac Defence -- [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, just for sake of fairness, could the witness be presented with paragraph 33 of the same statement which is also referring to the centre of Gracac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Are you invited, Ms. Mahindaratne, to put that to the witness, and if Ms. Mahindaratne would not do so, then I take that you will do it in cross-examination. Now, therefore, you know what will happen, Ms. Mahindaratne, if you don't do it, so therefore please consider to follow the suggestion.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I will do it, Mr. President, at the risk of losing time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Page 10 in English, third sentence.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Sacic, of course, you said you were not there. But I -- at the invitation of the Defence I'm going to read another part of what the witness said. You want me to read paragraph 33, Mr. Mikulicic, is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I'm referring to the third sentence of the paragraph, 33.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: "Between Gospic and Gracac 50 kilometres everything was destroyed. There was looting in several places. Burning was not going on in the centre of Gracac at that time. There were no civilians. In Gracac I saw men in khaki uniforms who said that they were with the MUP. Later on, at a press conference in Zagreb, Ivan Tolj had said this is normalisation, within quotes, 'I could not understand that.'" I just read that to you, Mr. Sacic, at the invitation of the Defence. I don't have a question -- [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, and that's what I observed. Would you tell me what it is that you expect of me.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I don't have a question in relation to that. I only read it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I am moving into the area which has to be examined under closed session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. One clarification as far as the last answer is concerned. You said that's what you observed after Ms. Mahindaratne had read to you that between Gospic and Gracac, 50 kilometres, everything was destroyed, there was looting in several places, burning -- one second, please. Burning was not going on in the centre of Gracac at that time. So by confirming that this is what you observed, there are two elements. First, is the description of the destruction between Gospic and Gracac, 50 kilometres, everything destroyed, looting in several places. That is one part of what she read to you. And the other part was that burning was not going on in the centre of Gracac at that time.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, absolutely not. 350 kilometres between Gospic and Gracac, even with my knowledge of geography, that is a bit extreme. Just that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There may be a problem of translation. Between Gospic and Gracac, 50 kilometres. So for that part of the country, everything destroyed, looting, several places. But no burning going on in Gracac. Now, what did you observe? Did you observe the destruction and the looting as well as no burning in the centre of Gracac; or was it one of these elements that were read to you, one or more? Did you observe large destruction between Gospic and Gracac, 50 kilometres? Did you observe that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did you see looting in several places?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I didn't see it, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm just trying to clarify your answer where you said, That's what I observed. Then I may I take it --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, 350 ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: First of all, it is about 50 kilometres, not 350. But did you want to confirm that you did not see -- that you did not observe burning in the centre of Gracac at that time? Is that what you confirmed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, what I'm confirming is that first I saw on the screen before me that it said 350 kilometres, nothing else. And now I don't see any of that anymore. But the Madam Prosecutor did say 350 kilometres, and then she corrected herself and said 50. Am I right? Did I hear you well just a moment ago?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We are talking about 50 kilometres. Please proceed with your answer. What did you now confirm from what was read to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That I did not see any destruction or looting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. And burning? No burning in Gracac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At that time, no, for sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So, as a matter of fact, you confirm not what was read to you, apart from the last portion. That is, that did you not observe burning in the centre of Gracac.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I saw, as I mentioned a couple of minutes ago a house burning. But I don't even know what day this refers to. This is a completely new statement that completely confuses me. I apologise, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think matters are sufficiently clear in this context. We move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. We will adjourn and resume tomorrow, the 25th of March, quarter past 2.00 in the afternoon, Courtroom I, but for the public already to know that it is extremely likely that we will move into private session almost immediately after we have started. We stand adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 25th day of March, 2010, at 2.15 p.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 7.07 p.m.,
